The function is strictly increasing where ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}(x-4),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
{x}^{2}(x-4)>0.
$$

The graph of $y={x}^{2}(x-4)$ has roots at $x=0$ and $x=4,$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/bfba80e21f4a458af6c4111191908a9d45d7d8c05f237db293cdad71a451d943.png)

Since ${x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all real $x,$ the product ${x}^{2}(x-4)$ is positive exactly when $x-4>0,$ that is, when $x>4.$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval 

$$
x>4.
$$
